name: Pasupatheeswarar Temple, Karur
deity: Shiva as Pasupatheeswarar (Aanilaiyappar), with the goddess Soundaranayaki (Alankaravalli)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Kongu country, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); Chola-era temple (11th-century inscriptions) with later additions
dynasty: Chola (inscriptions of Rajendra Chola) with later Tamil patrons
summary: Pasupatheeswarar Temple in ancient Karur, the Aanilai of the Tevaram on the Amaravati river, is a Chola-era Shiva shrine of the Kongu country, where Kamadhenu is said to have worshipped the Lord known as Aanilaiyappar and where the saint-composer Karuvur Thevar is remembered.

sections.history: Karur, the ancient Karuvur, is among the oldest cities of the Tamil country, known from Sangam-age literature and linked with the name Vanji, and it stands on the Amaravati river in the Kongu region. In the Tevaram the shrine is Karuvur Aanilai, counted among the seven Kongu Nadu temples praised by the saints, a Paadal Petra Sthalam sung by Sambandar and Sundarar. Inscriptions show that the temple was flourishing in the reign of Rajendra Chola (1012–1054 CE), who made a gift of land to it, and the oldest parts of the present masonry are assigned to the Chola period of the eleventh century. The shrine is also tied to the saint-composer Karuvur Thevar, credited with hymns of the Tiruvisaippa in the Tirumurai, and to the Nayanar Eripatha, for both of whom Karur is the sacred birthplace. Arunagirinathar too praised the Lord of this place.
sections.architecture: The temple is Dravidian in style and is entered through a five-tiered rajagopuram, which one source puts at about 120 feet. Its shrines stand within concentric walls of granite, and the gopuram, walls and pillars carry carved scenes from the puranas, in which some visitors read the blended influence of Chera, Chola and Pandya art. The sanctum of Pasupatheeswarar holds a swayambhu lingam, slightly leaning, which tradition connects with the saint Karuvur Thevar. The goddess is honoured as Soundaranayaki, and a second goddess, Kripanayaki, is named in temple tradition as the power of action beside her power of will. Among the other shrines, that of Adikesava Perumal is the most prominent, so that Shiva and Vishnu are worshipped within a single enclosure. The temple's sacred waters are the Brahma Teertham and the nearby Amaravati river.
sections.legends: The name Aanilai, the place of the cow, belongs to the temple's founding story. In the sthala tradition Brahma was given the work of creation and grew proud of it, and the task passed to Kamadhenu, the divine cow. On the advice of the sage Narada, Kamadhenu came to the forest of Vanji, where she found a lingam beneath an anthill and worshipped it until Shiva was pleased; the Lord came to be called Aanilaiyappar, Lord of the cow's abode. A second tradition belongs to the saint Karuvur Thevar: it is said that the Lord leaned slightly to one side to listen to his songs, and that the saint merged with Aanilaiyappar here, leaving the lingam inclined as it is seen today. Karur is also the town of the Nayanar Eripatha, remembered for his fierce devotion.
sections.festivals: The annual Brahmotsavam is held in the month of Panguni (mid-March to mid-April), and on three days in that month the rays of the sun are said to fall on the lingam. The Eripatha Nayanar festival commemorates the saint of Karur, Navaratri is celebrated in September and October, and Arudra Darshan in Margazhi (December–January) honours Shiva as Nataraja. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Come to Karur in the quiet of early morning, before the town wakes, and enter beneath the five-tiered gopuram. Walk the broad prakarams slowly, reading the carved stories on the pillars and walls, and come to the sanctum of Pasupatheeswarar, where the leaning lingam rewards a long look. Then visit the goddess Soundaranayaki in her own shrine and the shrine of Adikesava Perumal nearby. Many devotees pause at the sacred waters, and those who come in Panguni may see the sun's rays touch the lingam. Karur is a busy commercial town, but within the walls the temple keeps the stillness of an ancient shrine.

visit.timings: Typically open from about 6 a.m. until midday and again from about 4 p.m. until the evening, with a midday break; sources differ (6 to 12:30 and 4 to 9 in one, 6 to 11 and 4 to 8 in another), so confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Karur is a major town on the Amaravati river, well connected by road and rail, and Karur Junction railway station lies in the town close to the temple. Tiruchirappalli is about 80 km away and Coimbatore around 125 km, each with an airport. Frequent buses from across Tamil Nadu serve Karur, and the temple stands in the town, easily reached by local auto or taxi.
